doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Self-imposed challenges, Bela Fleck, Mingus and touring
summary: Levy likes challenges and kindred spirits like Bela Fleck, admires Mingus, says touring accelerates learning, and admits limits in sight-reading.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Do you think the most challenging musical situations that you’ve been in over the years, have they mostly been self-imposed? By that I mean well you’re playing with Bela and wow this is tricky music. But my observation is that you invent your own challenges.

Yeah. I mean if you get with someone who’s like a kindred spirit, I mean Bela and I very much so, both playing very unstandard things on our instruments, you know, especially the harmonica and the banjo. The piano is another thing. And so I love a challenge as long as I can rise to the challenge. If the challenge is beyond me I say like let someone else play the gig. But if it’s something I feel I can really sink my teeth into it’s like man, yeah, let’s go for it, let’s do this tune that has all these really odd changes in it and strange rhythmic modulations. Yeah it’s just like food you know. You grow as a human being from learning how to play all this stuff. I mean I’ve been listening to a bunch of Mingus lately. And I think that the guys who played with him, it was the same thing. The stuff he wrote was just so, like so wild and so emotionally spontaneous. And the fact that he could notate it all. And you know you play music like this, it transforms you you know? And it gives you a vocabulary that you wouldn’t have had before you played this music. And then there’s the other part of the question that you asked, it really relates directly to touring. Because I think that a musician really grows from touring and having to play similar material night after night after night and trying to remain creative but also stay within the music is sort of those two tensions for someone like me who’s always trying to find new things and also remaining faithful to the music. It’s the way you grow. It accelerates the learning process.

Can you think of a circumstance that happened to you, or you just mentioned that if you didn’t feel you could rise to a challenge you would suggest someone else do it. What kind of situation might that be?

Something where they’re asking me to read something on piano that a classical musician could read, and I’m looking at it going man, I can’t read all this stuff. You know. If you want me, if there’s some reading and some soloing involved yeah cool. But if you’re asking me to play stuff that would just take me way too long to learn, because my reading
has never been up to the level of my ability to improvise. I mean it’s not terrible – I’m a pretty good reader – but like yeah, that kind of thing.
